```{r, include = FALSE}
# The figures are drawn 9 inches wide, as in the Word report, and shrunk to
# the width of the page
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 9,
                      fig.height = 6, out.width = "100%")
```

```{r setup}
library(SurvFitSummary)
```

SurvFitSummary carries out the survival analyses that inform the inputs of
cost-effectiveness models for health technology assessment: it summarises
time-to-event data, fits the standard parametric models of NICE DSU
Technical Support Document 14 and Royston-Parmar spline models to each
treatment arm and to the arms together, extrapolates the survival beyond the
follow-up, and writes the results to an Excel workbook and a Word report.
This vignette goes through these steps with the example data of the package.
The models are described in more detail in
`vignette("models", package = "SurvFitSummary")`, and the validation of the
package in `vignette("validation", package = "SurvFitSummary")`.

## Data

The example data `fit_example.csv` were simulated for two arms of 300
patients, with the time to event in months (`AVAL`) and a censoring
indicator (`CNSR`, 1 = censored). `processing_dataset()` reads a data frame
or a file (CSV, Excel, SAS or SAS transport), renames the columns to `ARM`,
`SURVTIME` and `EVENT`, checks the values, and sets the control arm as the
first level of `ARM`.

```{r data}
path <- system.file("extdata", "fit_example.csv", package = "SurvFitSummary")
dat <- processing_dataset(path, column_arm = "TRT01P",
                          column_survtime = "AVAL", column_cnsr = "CNSR",
                          control_arm = "Control")
head(dat)
smry <- summarise_data(dat)
smry
```

```{r summary-values, include = FALSE}
ctrl <- smry[smry$ARM == "Control", ]
trt <- smry[smry$ARM == "Treatment", ]
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
```

The control arm has `r ctrl$n` patients with `r ctrl$events` events and a
median time to event of `r f1(ctrl$median)` months (95% CI
`r f1(ctrl$median_lcl)` to `r f1(ctrl$median_ucl)`); the treatment arm has
`r trt$events` events and a median of `r f1(trt$median)` months (95% CI
`r f1(trt$median_lcl)` to `r f1(trt$median_ucl)`).

## Kaplan-Meier estimates, hazard ratio and proportional hazards

`km_table()` gives the Kaplan-Meier estimates with their standard errors and
confidence intervals and the numbers at risk at regular times, and
`plot_km()` draws the curves with the numbers at risk; each curve ends at the
last observed time of its arm.

```{r km}
km <- km_table(dat, interval = 12)
head(km)
```

```{r km-plot, fig.height = 6.5}
plot_km(dat, conf_int = TRUE)
```

```{r hr}
hr <- estimate_hazard_ratio(dat)
hr
ph <- test_proportional_hazards(dat)
ph
```

The Cox model without adjustment gives a hazard ratio of `r f2(hr$hr[1])`
(95% CI `r f2(hr$lcl[1])` to `r f2(hr$ucl[1])`) for
`r hr$comparison[1]`. The Grambsch-Therneau test of the proportional hazards
assumption gives p = `r f3(ph$p_value[1])`. Covariates and strata of the
data can be added with the arguments `covariates` and `strata` of
`estimate_hazard_ratio()`.

## Diagnostics

The transformations of the Kaplan-Meier estimate that are linear in log time
for the Weibull, log-logistic and lognormal distributions, and the log of the
smoothed hazard that is linear in time for the Gompertz distribution,
indicate which distributions may describe each arm. The scaled Schoenfeld
residuals and the quantile-quantile plot of the two arms show whether the
hazards are proportional and whether the arms differ by a factor on the time
scale (accelerated failure time).

```{r diagnostics, fig.height = 8}
plot_distribution_diagnostics(dat)
```

```{r schoenfeld}
plot_schoenfeld(dat)
```

```{r qq, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 7.5, out.width = "75%"}
plot_qq_survival(dat)
```

## Fitting the models

`fit_survival_models()` fits, by default, the seven standard distributions
of NICE DSU TSD 14 and the spline models on the hazard, odds and normal
scales with 1 to 3 internal knots, to each arm (independent fits) and to
both arms with the arm as a covariate (dependent fits). A model that fails
or warns is recorded with its message, and the other models are still
fitted.

```{r fit}
fits <- fit_survival_models(dat)
fits
```

```{r fit-values, include = FALSE}
gof <- gof_table(fits)
best <- gof[!duplicated(paste(gof$fit_type, gof$arm)), ]
```

`r length(unique(fits$models$model))` models were fitted to each of the
`r length(unique(paste(fits$models$fit_type, fits$models$arm)))` data sets,
`r nrow(fits$models)` fits in all. `gof_table()` sorts the models of each fit
by AIC: the lowest AIC is that of the `r best$model[best$arm == "Control"]`
model for the control arm, the `r best$model[best$arm == "Treatment"]` model
for the treatment arm, and the `r best$model[best$arm == "Both arms"]` model
for both arms.

```{r gof}
head(gof[gof$arm == "Control", ], 6)
```

## Extrapolation

The models agree within the follow-up but can differ widely beyond it, which
is why the choice of the model for a cost-effectiveness model rests on the
plausibility of the extrapolation as well as on the fit.
`predict_survival()` gives the survival (or the hazard) of each model at
given times, with the Kaplan-Meier estimate where the data reach.

```{r predict}
pred <- predict_survival(fits, times = c(12, 60, 120))
ctrl_pred <- pred[pred$fit_type == "independent" & pred$arm == "Control", ]
head(ctrl_pred[ctrl_pred$time == 120, c("model", "time", "est", "km")], 8)
```

```{r predict-values, include = FALSE}
s120 <- ctrl_pred$est[ctrl_pred$time == 120]
```

For the control arm, the survival at 10 years ranges from `r f3(min(s120))`
to `r f3(max(s120))` across the `r length(s120)` models.

```{r survival-fits, fig.height = 7.5}
plot_survival_fits(fits, arms = "Control",
                   models = c("Exponential", "Weibull", "Log-logistic",
                              "Lognormal", "Hazards, 1 knot"),
                   time_horizon = 120)
```

```{r hazard-fits, fig.height = 6.5}
plot_hazard_fits(fits, arms = "Control",
                 models = c("Exponential", "Weibull", "Log-logistic",
                            "Lognormal", "Hazards, 1 knot"),
                 time_horizon = 120)
```

The legend is below the plot by default; `legend_position = "right"` (or
`"top"`, `"left"`, `"none"`) places it elsewhere, in all the plots of the
package.

## Excel workbook and Word report

`write_survival_workbook()` writes the tables of the analysis to an Excel
workbook, one table per sheet: the data summary, the Kaplan-Meier table, the
hazard ratios, the proportional hazards test, the status of the models, the
fit statistics, the parameters on the natural and transformed scales with
the rows of their covariance matrices, the covariance matrices and their
Cholesky factors, the survival summary, the predicted survival at the
landmark times and the knots of the spline models.

```{r workbook}
workbook <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
write_survival_workbook(fits, workbook, conf_int = FALSE)
file.exists(workbook)
unlink(workbook)
```

`write_survival_report()` writes a Word report with the methods, the
diagnostics, the fits of the standard parametric and spline models with
their tables and figures (with and without confidence intervals), and the
extrapolations. With all the models it takes a few minutes, because each
figure is drawn as an image.

```{r report, eval = FALSE}
write_survival_report(fits, "survival_report.docx",
                      outcome = "Overall survival")
```
